item.title: On the Nature of the BeWD System Nova FQ Circinus
item.description: arXiv:2610.26957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical nova FQ Cir (Schaefer et al. 2026) has recently been shown to have a Be star donor, and has been identified as a High Mass Cataclysmic Variable (HMCV), with an orbital period of $\sim 2.04d$ (twice the 1.02d periodogram peak). Using the extensive OGLE optical archive, together with existing observations from ASAS-SN we instead find significant modulation between $\sim 50-60$~days and propose that the orbital period is likely closer to $\sim 62d$. We interpret the low amplitude 1.02 d modulation as a non-radial pulsation of the Be star. We also reassess the HMCV classification based on properties of known Be star-white dwarf systems.

item.title: Slowly Rotating Fully Convective Stars at $\lesssim$ 1 Gyr: Evidence from the Hyades and Praesepe
item.description: arXiv:2610.27112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the discovery of 10 stars in the Praesepe and Hyades clusters with unusually slow rotation that are likely not field contamination. Even though our search was general, all slow rotators are in the fully convective domain. We find that the fraction of slow rotators in the clusters is more than $5\sigma$ above the distribution expected from field contamination. They provide a potential link between the period distribution of the young open clusters and the field. These stars could be a distinct birth population, or they could be an indication that the onset of strong magnetic breaking is earlier than previously realized in this domain. Photometric variability and X-ray luminosity suggest the later but more data is needed to confirm. Searches for similar populations in younger clusters will help determine when slow rotators first emerge and constrain the timescale and physical mechanisms governing angular-momentum loss in fully convective stars. The discovery of these stars also highlights the importance of long-baseline photometric observations for detecting the long rotation periods of low-mass stars.
item.dc:creator: Yuxi Lu, Marc H. Pinsonneault, Jos\'e G. Fern\'andez-Trincado, Richard R. Lane, Alexandre Roman-Lopes, Keivan G. Stassun, Emily K. Pass, Guy S. Stringfellow

item.title: 20,000 Rotation Periods in Nearby Open Clusters and Moving Groups from ZTF and ASAS-SN
item.description: arXiv:2610.27113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open clusters provide uniquely powerful laboratories for studying stellar evolution because their members share a common age and chemical composition. Stellar rotation of low-mass GKM dwarfs in open clusters provides direct empirical constraints on magnetic braking, with implications for stellar interiors, magnetic activity, and star--planet interactions. However, existing cluster rotation samples are dominated by space-based observations, whose limited spatial coverage and short observing baselines can make it difficult to construct an unbiased sample. Long-baseline ground-based time-domain surveys therefore provide an important complement to space-based photometry. I present a catalog of $\sim$20,000 periodic photometric signals, including stellar rotations, eclipsing-binaries, and classical pulsators, measured from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN) for members of nearby open clusters and moving groups within 1.5 kpc. This catalog provides a new empirical foundation for studying the mass, chemical composition, and age dependence of stellar angular-momentum evolution and for testing models of magnetic braking across a broad range of stellar masses and evolutionary states.
item.dc:creator: Yuxi Lu

item.title: Evolution of Massive Main-Sequence Stars in Binary Population Synthesis. II. Consequences for Black Hole High-Mass X-ray Binaries and Binary Black Holes
item.description: arXiv:2610.27186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactions and mass loss during the main-sequence (MS) phase of massive binary stars can significantly alter their subsequent evolution and the properties of the black holes (BHs) they ultimately produce. We use the rapid binary population synthesis code \textsc{COMPAS}, incorporating a new treatment of MS evolution that self-consistently tracks the convective core under arbitrary mass-loss or mass-gain histories. We explore the properties of black hole high-mass X-ray binaries (BH-HMXBs) and binary black holes (BBHs) formed under this new framework. We find that a more detailed treatment of MS evolution is necessary to reproduce the high BH masses observed in BH-HMXBs, which are otherwise absent under prescriptions that do not take the internal structure of MS stars into account. Matching the observed rates and orbital periods favors case A mass transfer that is more non-conservative than commonly assumed. We further find that mass transfer of helium-enriched material during case A mass transfer is common in massive binaries, with potential consequences for the structure of the accreting star. For the BBH population, the new MS framework alters the chirp-mass and mass-ratio distributions of detectable mergers, and case A mass transfer can make a substantial contribution to the BBHs formed through the stable mass transfer channel. These systems show a strong preference for near-equal mass ratios, broadly consistent with recent constraints from gravitational-wave observations.
item.dc:creator: Adam Br\v{c}ek, Ryosuke Hirai, Ilya Mandel, Jack Yutong Chen

item.title: Large-scale Vortices in the Solar Photosphere: Statistical Properties and the Reliability of Local Correlation Tracking
item.description: arXiv:2610.27222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vortices are observed throughout the solar atmosphere, spanning a wide range of spatial scales. Although small-scale vortices have been studied extensively, mesoscale vortices remain less explored, and it is still unclear whether they can be reliably recovered from observations. Mesogranular-scale motions are recovered from the R2D2 simulations by applying Gaussian spatial smoothing to the horizontal velocity field with full width at half maximum (FWHM) values of 2.5-4.0 Mm. To evaluate the accuracy of local correlation tracking (LCT) and its suitability for identifying mesogranular vortices, we apply LCT to synthetic intensity maps at $\tau = 1$ using the same spatial windows and temporal averaging windows of 10-60 minutes. Vortices are identified in both the reference and LCT-derived velocity fields using the $\Gamma$ method. For all tested parameter combinations, LCT underestimates the number of mesogranular-scale vortices. The best overall recovery is obtained for relatively small spatial smoothing scales (FWHM $\leq 3.5$ Mm) and short averaging windows ($\leq 20$ minutes), which provide the most reliable vorticity and lifetime statistics while maintaining strong agreement in vortex radius and area distributions. Our analysis shows that only a modest fraction of LCT-detected vortices correspond to vortices identified in the reference velocity field (3.54%-17.88%), depending on FWHM and temporal averaging. This indicates that vortex-driven dynamics inferred from LCT-detected vortices should be interpreted with caution. Our results suggest that applying the $\Gamma$ method to LCT-derived velocity fields can recover useful statistical properties of mesoscale vortical structures, especially their temporal trends and characteristic sizes.
item.dc:creator: Mashael Aldhafeeri, Suzana S. A. Silva, Istvan Ballai, Gary Verth, Haruhisa Iijima, Hideyuki Hotta, Viktor Fedun

item.title: Phakoseismology: Asteroseismology of gravitationally microlensed stars
item.description: arXiv:2610.28005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asteroseismology relies on disk-integrated photometry or radial velocities, in which geometric cancellation suppresses modes of high spherical degree ($l\geq4$). Observations are thus limited to deeply penetrating, low-degree modes, leaving the outer envelope inaccessible. We investigate whether a high-magnification microlensing event can temporarily lift this limitation by differentially magnifying the surface of an oscillating source star. We modelled the visibility of solar-like oscillations during microlensing, weighting the surface by limb darkening and the local magnification. We computed multiplet visibilities and the power distribution among azimuthal components, and built a likelihood model for recovering the 3D spin-axis orientation from resolved rotational multiplets. When the lens-source separation becomes comparable to the source's angular radius, the magnification gradient acts as a transient spatial filter that breaks the symmetry of disk integration, raising high-degree mode visibilities by up to three orders of magnitude. The same non-axisymmetric weighting makes the relative power of azimuthal components depend on both the inclination and sky-projected azimuth of the spin axis, imprinting the full spin orientation onto the power spectrum. With $5\%$ relative-power uncertainties, we recover the orientation to $\sigma_i=2.9^\circ$ and $\sigma_\gamma=11.5^\circ$. Microlensing thus does more than amplify distant stars: its magnification pattern enables spatially selective asteroseismology. The effect is strongest for rare close encounters and unlikely to support large samples, and the newly visible high-degree modes will overlap with rotationally split and mixed modes, complicating mode identification. Nevertheless, individual high-quality events may open a window on envelope physics and spin geometries for stars in the Galactic bulge and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Marcus L. Marcussen, Mikkel N. Lund

item.title: Deriving Interplanetary Sector Boundary Crossings using Potential Field Source Surface Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.28123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS) and associated interplanetary sector boundaries fundamentally structure the solar wind environment, modulating coronal mass ejection (CME) evolution and solar energetic particle transport. In this study, we evaluate the capability of a static Potential Field Source Surface (PFSS; $R_{ss}=2.5R_\odot$) coronal model to directly map interplanetary sector boundary crossings from the Sun to 1 au without dynamic heliospheric propagation models. We compare ballistically transported HCS crossings derived from GONG-ADAPT and SDO/HMI magnetic maps against sector boundary crossing observations from the SBCross catalog. PFSS modeling reproduces the large-scale interplanetary magnetic field topology well ($J\approx0.50$), achieving hit rates (POD) of 0.64 for GONG-ADAPT and 0.76 for HMI. Carrington synoptic maps outperform flux-transport modeled maps, suggesting that the short-term observational noise from data assimilation degrades topological matching more than map "aging". Predictive skill shows a strong solar cycle dependence, performing significantly better during solar maxima (POD=0.70-0.81) than solar minima (POD=0.56-0.67), attributed to more distinct crossings due to higher HCS inclination angles during maximum. Matched events exhibit travel times close to ballistic estimates of 4.8-4.9 days with an average timing difference centered near zero ($\pm1.1$ days) and 90% of events within $\pm 1.8$ days. The hit rate of HCS structures that interact with CMEs does not degrade (POD = 0.67-0.83), despite propagating $\approx7$ hours faster on average, implying that the CME interaction causes only minor structural changes to the HCS. Larger timing differences (>24 hours) are associated with flatter current sheets. Overall, static PFSS extrapolations offer a computationally inexpensive, effective approach for mapping global sector boundary structure.
item.dc:creator: Stephan G. Heinemann, Manuela Temmer, Jens Pomoell, Mathew Owens, Emilia Kilpua, Matti ala-Lahti, Andreas Wagner

item.title: Detection and Statistics of large-scale Sector Boundary Crossings in the Solar Wind: The SBCross Catalog
item.description: arXiv:2610.28139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Heliospheric sector boundary crossings (SBCs), composed of the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS), Heliospheric Plasma Sheet (HPS), and surrounding plasma halo, represent fundamental structures in the solar wind that influence interplanetary dynamics and space weather. We present the \textsc{SBCross} catalog, an automated, publicly available database containing 1,076 SBC events derived from in-situ observations spanning more than 30 years (1995--2026), covering Solar Cycles 23 and 24 alongside the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. By combining interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and 255~eV suprathermal electron pitch angle distributions (PAD) data, our algorithm reliably captures large-scale polarity transitions, with $76\%$ of detected SBCs exhibiting clear HPS signatures ($\beta > 1$, $n_{\mathrm{peak}} > 10\mathrm{\,cm^{-3}}$). Across the catalog, we find an average occurrence rate of $\approx 2.6$ events per Carrington rotation, a median event duration of $\approx 9.0$\,hours, and a median physical thickness of $\approx 7.4 \times 10^6$\,km. Furthermore, approximately $\approx 15\%$ of detected SBCs interact with interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs) on average, with this proportion rising up to $33\%$ during solar maximum. These CME-associated events exhibit systematically longer durations (median of $10.0$\,hours), $54\%$ larger physical thicknesses, and higher average solar wind velocities. Notably, all high-velocity SBC events ($> 600\mathrm{\,km\,s^{-1}}$) are exclusively driven by CME interactions, demonstrating local plasma pile-up and structural entanglement resulting from fast CMEs overtaking the ambient slow background. The \textsc{SBCross} catalog serves as an updated successor to the classic SBC list by L. Svalgaard, delivering a standardized, open-access resource for the heliophysics community to systematically investigate sector boundary transitions.
item.dc:creator: Stephan G. Heinemann, Manuela Temmer, Mathew Owens, Emilia Kilpua, Charles Farrugia, Daniel Price

item.title: Orbital Parameters for 65 Wide Binary Systems: no evidence for gravitational anomaly at low acceleration
item.description: arXiv:2610.28220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use a Monte Carlo analysis to study whether wide binaries can be represented by bound Newtonian orbits, and, if this is the case, whether the distribution of the orbital parameters agrees with expectations. The potential orbits are classified according to the $\chi^2$ probability of representing star coordinates, parallaxes, velocity components and masses. We apply this analysis to 44 systems previously published, to which we add 26 wide binaries, consisting of twin low-mass (M) stars. We find orbital solutions for 65 systems, and derive the distribution of their orbital parameters. For one system composed of M-type stars, no Newtonian bound solution can be found; however, this pair is a member of the young Argus association and therefore not a suitable target. The remaining four systems that cannot be fit were already identified as likely disrupted binaries. The uncertainty in the separation between the components, given by the parallax error, is by far the dominant error source, and the main limitation of the present analysis, affecting especially the determination of the orbits' inclination angle and phase. Newtonian dynamics describe well our sample. When dividing the sample into two subsamples, according to the mutual acceleration, the eccentricity and periastron distributions agree with theoretical expectations; inclination and phase are distorted by the parallax-limited separation, more strongly in the high-acceleration (37 systems) than in the low-acceleration ($A_N < 10^{-9} m s^{-2}$, 28 systems) subsample, which is opposite to what a gravitational signal would produce. In particular the ratio between observed velocity difference and circular velocity does not show any excess for the low acceleration sample. When parametrized as a boost $\gamma$ parameter to the velocity, $0.95 < \gamma <1.05 (1 \sigma)$, fully consistent with Newton also for the low acceleration sample.
item.dc:creator: L. Pasquini, R. Saglia, F. Patat, L. Berni, D. Bossini, L. Magrini, H. -G. Ludwig, M. T. Murphy, J. R. de Medeiros, B. L. Canto Martins, J. Chanam\'e

item.title: The Effect of Field Line Tracing Height on Wang-Sheeley-Arge Solar Wind Predictions at Earth
item.description: arXiv:2610.28274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: (Abridged abstract): A key component of the widely used Wang-Sheeley-Arge model is the tracing of magnetic field lines in the solar corona, as that largely determines the modeled open/closed field regions and in turn the predicted large-scale solar wind structure. We demonstrate that by slightly raising the height from which magnetic field lines are traced from the photosphere (R$_{su}$), we can improve the prediction of solar wind high-speed enhancements (HSEs). We find a higher R$_{su}$ produces more accurate estimates of the HSE start time, duration, and peak speed, and enables the detection of HSEs that were missed with the standard R$_{su}$. These improvements are primarily associated with changes in the great-circle angular distance, while the flux tube expansion factors remain largely unchanged. A higher R$_{su}$ produces smoother open-field boundaries and reduces small-scale fragmentation within open-field regions. These morphological changes lead to more stable magnetic footpoint mappings and consequently more robust GCD calculations. To assess the statistical relevance of these findings, we extend the analysis to 53 Carrington rotations and perform a multi-metric evaluation of model performance. The results indicate that higher R$_{su}$ improves HSE predictions while reducing false alarms. We thus find that the choice of R$_{su}$ represents an important and previously underexplored parameter that can help enhance our ambient solar wind modeling and forecasting capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Satabdwa Majumdar, Martin A. Reiss, Pete Riley, Charles N. Arge

item.title: Real-Time 24-hour Ahead Forecasting of Solar Energetic Particle Events with SEPNET-PRISM-R
item.description: arXiv:2610.28292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events, operationally defined as proton flux exceeding 10 pfu in the >10 MeV channel, threaten spacecraft systems, astronaut safety, and high latitude aviation, yet continuous real-time forecasting with adequate lead time remains difficult. We present SEPNET-PRISM-R, a near-real-time system that issues hourly, 24 hour ahead probabilistic SEP forecasts. The model integrates multimodal solar data - including active region patches, flare features, coronal mass ejection (CME) characteristics, and historical proton flux - to concurrently predict SEP occurrences, peak proton flux, soft X-ray flux, and CME velocity, with the primary objective being SEP forecasting. Building on existing literature, SEPNET-PRISM-R enhances operational performance by incorporating a postprocessing module that enables cross-validated decision making and interpretable quantification of feature importance. The training dataset spans from February 1986 to September 2025, with subsequent forecasts generated sequentially through the present via a real-time space weather prediction platform that provides predictive probabilities, feature attributions, and historical analogs, enabling more reliable and informed operational decision-making. The proposed framework substantially suppresses false alarm rates while maintaining robust event detection capabilities, as evidenced by case studies and aggregate statistics.
item.dc:creator: Yian Yu, Yang Chen, Lulu Zhao, Kathryn Whitman, Ward Manchester, Tamas Gombosi

item.title: Coevolution of Dust Growth and Gravitational Instability in Massive Protostellar Disks
item.description: arXiv:2610.28331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Massive protostellar disks are expected to sustain high accretion rates through gravitational instability, while dust growth may modify their opacity, cooling efficiency, and stability. Conversely, the time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric structures produced by gravitational instability may regulate the local conditions for dust growth. However, the coupled evolution of dust growth and gravitational instability in massive protostellar disks has not yet been explored self-consistently. We present two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that follow gas dynamics, dust growth, and opacity-dependent radiative cooling in a massive protostellar disk. We find that dust grains rapidly grow to millimeter-centimeter sizes shortly after disk formation, substantially reducing the infrared opacity. The enhanced cooling promotes disk fragmentation and produces more frequent accretion-driven luminosity outbursts than in a model without dust growth, with durations and peak luminosities comparable to those observed in massive protostars. Dust growth is broadly regulated by the fragmentation-limited size in dense disk regions, whereas newly formed outer disk regions and low-density regions deviate from this limit because of finite collision timescales and dust transport. These results suggest that dust growth may facilitate episodic accretion and fragmentation, while gravitationally unstable disk structures in turn regulate the dust growth process.
item.dc:creator: Ryota Yamamuro, Ryoki Matsukoba, Kei E. I. Tanaka, Eduard I. Vorobyov

item.title: Data-Driven Ages from Asteroseismology for FGK Dwarfs
item.description: arXiv:2610.28345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Age is the one of the most difficult stellar properties to constrain. However, upcoming surveys such as PLATO are about to revolutionize our ability to measure FGK dwarf ages with asteroseismology. Here, we use The Cannon to construct a data-driven model for inferring asteroseismic-quality age measurements from large spectroscopic survey observations and demonstrate that forthcoming asteroseismology datasets from future surveys can be leveraged, together with our model, to obtain stellar age samples larger than can be obtained by those surveys alone. We train The Cannon on 323 FGK dwarf stars with asteroseismic age labels from NASA Kepler photometry and high-resolution spectra from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE). We apply our model to FGK dwarfs from the Kepler survey that exhibit solar-like oscillations and reproduce their reported asteroseismic-quality ages with an RMS scatter of 1.0 Gyr. We then apply our model to the sample of 3810 Kepler FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra to infer data-driven asteroseismic ages. We repeat this for the larger sample of 48,828 FGK dwarfs with APOGEE spectra. Our work demonstrates that data-driven methods can robustly reproduce asteroseismic ages for FGK dwarfs. These methods will be invaluable tools for extending asteroseimology measurements from upcoming surveys (e.g., PLATO) to much larger stellar samples.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Lam, Aida Behmard, Sarah Ballard, Andrew R. Casey, Jamie N. Tayar, Jared A. Goldberg

item.title: Photometric variability of blue supergiants: Constraints on stellar masses and evolutionary stages
item.description: arXiv:2610.28352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blue supergiants (BSGs) are crucial to understanding the evolution of massive stars. Although distinguishing between pre- and post-red supergiant (RSG) phases is challenging, stellar pulsations provide valuable constraints on their masses and evolutionary status. This study analyzes TESS light curves of six BSGs with high L/M to identify periodicities. We performed theoretical modeling of the radial unstable modes to characterize the strange modes. We aim to estimate asteroseismic masses, compare them with spectroscopic and evolutionary mass estimates, and assess the evolutionary stage of the stars. We employed the Lomb-Scargle periodogram and the weighted wavelet Z-transform to address quasiperiodic behavior and time-varying signals. A linear nonadiabatic stability analysis was performed to test for radial perturbations, generating eigenfrequencies that enable stellar mass estimation. In addition, we characterized the stochastic low-frequency variability (SLFV). We derive a first guess at the asteroseismic masses. We find that HD 74371 and HD 79186 are evolving blueward following the RSG phase, while the evolutionary stage of HD 115842 cannot be uniquely determined with the available mass estimates. We also find that HD 52382 and HD 99953 are likely in the post-RSG phase; however, their low masses are difficult to reconcile with the available evolutionary models. The extreme supergiant HD 80077 shows the largest mass discrepancy in the sample, suggesting a more complex evolutionary history. The SLFV properties do not provide a clear diagnostic of the evolutionary stage. These results highlight the potential of asteroseismology as a complementary tool for constraining the evolutionary status of BSGs. However, the mass discrepancies found for some objects indicate that additional observational and theoretical efforts are required.
item.dc:creator: A. Alberici Adam, L. S. Cidale, M. Kourniotis, W. Glatzel, J. P. S\'anchez Arias, M. Ru\'iz D\'iaz, A. Christen

item.title: Tight asteroseismic upper limits on hot subdwarf magnetism
item.description: arXiv:2610.28443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The apparent absence of magnetism in subdwarf B stars (sdBs) has emerged as an outstanding observational puzzle, especially in light of their likely origin in binary interactions. Gravity-mode pulsations in some sdBs offer a unique opportunity to extend recent successes in asteroseismic magnetic field detection in red giants. In the presence of strong magnetic fields, gravity modes are expected to be significantly damped, suppressing their observed amplitudes. We place stringent upper limits on magnetic fields in 30 hot subdwarfs by using the observation of low-frequency dipole and quadrupole modes to rule out magnetic suppression. Even under conservative assumptions, our upper limits constrain near-surface magnetic fields to below a kilogauss in roughly half of our sample, with the strongest individual constraint reaching down to $\sim20\,\mathrm{G}$. These upper limits reinforce the apparent dearth of magnetic fields in hot subdwarfs and demonstrate asteroseismology as a powerful new probe of magnetism in these stars.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Z. Rui, Linhao Ma

item.title: Resonant three-mode coupling in asteroseismology I: Bifurcations, chaos, and DAV white-dwarf outbursts
item.description: arXiv:2610.28513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resonant three-mode coupling is a fundamental nonlinear process in stellar oscillations and other wave systems. We investigate the global dynamics of a linearly overstable parent mode coupled to two damped daughter modes. The principal control parameters are frequency detuning $\Delta$ and daughter damping rate $\Gamma$, normalized by the parent growth rate. We combine high-resolution maps of the largest Lyapunov exponent in the $(\Gamma,\Delta)$ plane with linear stability analysis, Floquet calculations, and numerical continuation. The resulting parameter space includes stable equilibria, simple and period-doubled limit cycles, chaotic attractors, formally unbounded solutions, and higher-period `shrimp' islands within chaotic regions. Successive period doublings lead to chaos, while boundaries of isolated periodic windows exhibit type-I intermittency. At large $\Gamma$, the main bifurcation boundaries approach straight lines, indicating that the dynamics is governed primarily by $r=\Delta/(2\Gamma)$. We connect finite-$\Gamma$ bifurcations to an earlier one-dimensional return map. As $\epsilon\rightarrow0$, this map recovers the principal period-doubling sequence, the onset of chaos near $r\simeq0.38$, and the asymptotic positions of prominent periodic windows. We also examine the effects of unequal daughter damping rates. Applying these results to sporadic outbursts in cool DAV white dwarfs, we find that estimated $g$-mode growth rates, damping rates, and detunings place resonant triplets in both periodic and chaotic regimes. Thus, instability of the three-mode equilibrium need not produce a regular limit cycle: deterministic chaos and intermittency may contribute to irregular outburst amplitudes and recurrence times.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Guo, Gordon I. Ogilvie

item.title: Automated optimization of solar energetic particle acceleration and transport parameters against five-spacecraft observations of the 9 October 2021 event
item.description: arXiv:2610.28603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events threaten space infrastructure, yet physics-based prediction models depend on numerous poorly constrained free parameters. We introduce the Fujitsu Solar Energetic particle Intelligent Tuning and Evaluation Network (SEITEN), which couples the SUSANOO MHD model of CME propagation to SEPIF, a diffusive shock acceleration and focused transport model, through the shock conditions SUSANOO supplies, and automatically optimizes the free parameters of the particle model against the SEP event of 9 October 2021. The mean free path and the injection efficiency vary independently along each magnetic field line and heliolongitudinal bin, giving a 19-dimensional problem solved by quasi-Monte Carlo sampling followed by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. The optimized model reproduces proton flux profiles at five spacecraft with a mean absolute error of $\approx 0.45$ in $\log_{10}$ flux, and the inferred mean free paths show a clear east-west structure; these are effective parameters conditional on the assumed transport geometry. Six independent runs show that whether mean free paths or injection efficiencies dominate depends on the MHD shock strength, and that injection efficiencies differ by orders of magnitude between MHD configurations despite nearly identical fit quality. Joint MHD-SEP parameter estimation is therefore a necessary next step towards generalized, operational SEP forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Hiroyuki Tako Ishikawa, Naho Fujita, Yuta Kato, Miki Kurihara, Takashi Minoshima, Daikou Shiota, Kazumasa Iwai, Marco Pinto, Ant\'onio Pessanha Gomes, Go Murakami, Kanya Kusano, Chihiro Mitsuda

item.title: Planets surviving common envelope evolution should be rare, massive, and orbit very close to their host star
item.description: arXiv:2610.27055v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The discovery of exoplanets around white dwarfs uniquely informs our understanding of planetary survival through stellar evolution. Common Envelope (CE) evolution is one of the proposed mechanisms that could shape the orbital architecture of these planets around stellar remnants. In this work, we predict the occurrence rate and orbital separation/planet mass distributions for planets that could form around white dwarfs through CE evolution. We simulate populations of giant-planet systems, sampling initial conditions from observed mass and semi-major axis distributions for main sequence stars. We evolve the host star from main sequence to white dwarf to assess which planetary configurations could survive, and we predict the resulting post-CE planet population. Our results suggest that such planets should be rare, massive, and have very close orbital separations. We find that most of the surviving planets have masses of $>10\,M_{\rm{Jup}}$ and orbital separations $<1.4$ times the tidal disruption radius, $a_{{disrupt}}$ ($\lesssim0.006$ AU, also called the Roche limit), which is in contrast to high eccentricity migration, which produces planets with orbital separations $>2a_{disrupt}$. The properties of CE survivors from our simulations contrast with the known closely-orbiting planet WD 1856+534 b, suggesting a different mechanism may be responsible for its formation.
item.dc:creator: Yadira S. Gaibor, Andrew Vanderburg, Juliette C. Becker, Melinda Soares-Furtado, Saul Rappaport, Tansu Daylan

item.title: Localizing binary neutron stars with the Einstein Telescope: a full Bayesian comparison of the triangular and 2L configurations
item.description: arXiv:2610.27081v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Einstein Telescope (ET), the European next-generation gravitational-wave observatory, is at a decisive stage: the choice of its detector configuration is still open, with profound implications for its scientific output. We provide a quantitative basis for this choice by comparing two candidate configurations at their proposed sites: the triangular design ($\Delta$) at the Euregio Meuse-Rhine site, and the 2L design, with interferometers in Sardinia, Italy, and Lusatia, Germany. We present the first realistic estimates of sky-localization uncertainties for binary neutron star (BNS) mergers, moving beyond Fisher-matrix forecasts to full Bayesian parameter estimation that captures the multimodal structure of the sky posterior. We focus mainly on the high-frequency interferometers alone, providing an expected scenario for the first years of ET operations, as the more challenging low-frequency instruments will come online later. BNS injections span different sky positions and luminosity distances between 40 and 2000 Mpc, corresponding to signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from 12 to 720. Our analysis relaxes the long-wavelength approximation and includes Earth's rotation and higher-order modes, all of which improve sky localization. We find that the $\Delta$ configuration localizes low- and moderate-SNR sources in eight degenerate sky modes spread across both hemispheres and over the day and night sides of the Earth, with 90% credible areas reaching $\sim 2 \times 10^4 \, \mathrm{deg}^2$. In contrast, the 2L configuration recovers a single dominant mode that contains at least 50% of the posterior probability and is one to two orders of magnitude smaller in area. This represents a substantial advantage for multimessenger follow-up campaigns.
item.dc:creator: Filippo Santoliquido, Jacopo Tissino, Marica Branchesi, Ulyana Dupletsa

item.title: The Imprint of Core-collapse Asymmetries on Supernova Shock Breakout
item.description: arXiv:2610.27183v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Shock breakout is the first electromagnetic signal of a supernova, generating a highly luminous and fast-timescale burst of thermal radiation. Motivated by recent theoretical progress in producing successful three-dimensional supernova explosions of massive stars, we undertake a detailed numerical study on the impact that the core-collapse asymmetries might have on the breakout signal. We perform the first fully 3D multi-group radiation hydrodynamics simulations of shock breakout for the case of a red supergiant explosion. We find that large-scale asymmetries formed during the core-collapse process can extend the breakout flash duration to days, with the timescale set by the supernova shock fully wrapping around the progenitor star. Using detailed 3D radiative transfer post-processing, we generate synthetic multi-wavelength light curves and spectra to more closely connect to observations. The light curves show a significant viewing-angle dependence of the overall shape and peak brightness of shock breakout. We find that core-collapse asymmetries have the largest impact on the breakout light curve when observed in shorter UV wavelengths. On the other hand, at optical wavelengths, we find a diminished impact of the asymmetric breakout that more closely resembles a 1D spherical breakout. Our results show how multi-dimensional effects originating from the core-collapse mechanism can play a major role in setting the shock breakout properties, and are particularly relevant to upcoming UV space missions such as ULTRASAT and UVEX.
item.dc:creator: David K. Khatami, David Vartanyan, Hai P. Le, Daniel N. Kasen, Adam Burrows

item.title: J-PLUS: Identifying Outlier Spectral Energy Distributions in the Fourth Data Release Using Unsupervised Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.27252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The selection of candidates belonging to rare or underrepresented stellar populations, as well as novel objects, is essential for spectroscopic follow-up. In this work, we demonstrate how combining broad- and narrow-band photometric information with machine-learning techniques enables this selection. Using photometric data in twelve filters from the Javalambre Photometric Local Universe Survey (J-PLUS) as input, we applied an anomaly detection technique based on autoencoders to identify spectral energy distributions (SEDs) that deviate from the dominant pattern in the J-PLUS objects sample. Subsequently, we applied the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) algorithm to the J-PLUS colors of the outlier SEDs population. Combining information from the SIMBAD database and other astronomical surveys to classify the outliers identified by the autoencoder, we are able to characterize over-densities in the t-SNE map. Our study specifically focuses on well-defined islands in the t-SNE space, corresponding to specific populations. We identified a large sample of white dwarfs and low-mass stars, including a small subset of polluted white dwarfs, and report potential candidates for spectroscopic follow-up, including 19 carbon-rich stars, 11 cataclysmic variables and 170 white-dwarfs-main-sequence binaries, all previously unreported in the literature.

item.title: SN 2023iop: An Extreme 1987A-like Supernova and the Death of Very Massive Stars
item.description: arXiv:2610.27312v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Supernova (SN) 1987A showed that some hydrogen-rich core-collapse supernovae (SNe) rise slowly to peak, defining a distinct subclass. Wide-field surveys have uncovered more extreme members, such as OGLE-2014-SN-73, SN 2020faa, and SN 2023vbw, that challenge neutrino-driven explosion models. We present ultraviolet-to-infrared, radio, X-ray, and spectropolarimetric observations of SN 2023iop at $z = 0.1020$, the most extreme 87A-like event to date. It rose for $\gtrsim88$ rest-frame days to $M_r \approx -20.1$ mag, also placing it among the hydrogen-rich superluminous SNe, and radiated $\gtrsim4\times10^{50}$ erg. Its spectra resemble those of typical Type II SNe and remain photospheric at $\sim330$ days post-maximum. Continuum polarization of 0.8-1.0% indicates an aspherical system. Hydrogen-rich pair-instability supernova (PISN) models of a $190~M_\odot$ star reproduce the light-curve up to 150 days after peak, but not the late-time emission. A late-time spectrum shows a feature near 7300 {\AA}, tentatively identified as [Ni II] $\lambda$7378. The implied $\approx0.02~M_\odot$ of stable $^{58}$Ni is reached only in the most massive PISN models. The low-mass host galaxy ($\sim10^{8.2}~M_\odot$) is consistent with a metal-poor progenitor as required by the PISN channel. Fallback accretion reproduces the light-curve morphology, but not the colors. We consider a pair-instability explosion the most plausible scenario, with the late-time light-curve excess powered by circumstellar interaction, which shows no signatures in the spectra. SN 2023iop shows that the most luminous 87A-like events occupy an underexplored region of massive-star evolution.

item.title: Exomoonlight Sonata: On the Fate of Exomoons Around Migrating White Dwarf Planets
item.description: arXiv:2610.27484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The survival of exomoons around close-in white dwarf planets offers a potential constraint on their migration histories and an alternative pathway to post-main-sequence habitability. We investigate whether moons can survive the tidal circularization of planets via high-eccentricity migration, and consider a hierarchical three-body system (white dwarf-planet-moon) after an initial eccentricity excitation of the planetary orbit. Using an analytic equilibrium tidal model, we compare the evolution of the planetary and satellite orbits and examine the conditions required for an evection resonance. We show that the moons of pseudosynchronously rotating planets always migrate inwards since the planetary corotation radius always exceeds the Hill radius, independent of mass and orbital eccentricities. Comparing the migration timescales for the moon and the planet shows that compact moons undergo rapid tidal decay relative to the outer orbit. However, the wider separations favored by slower migration timescales experience pericenter perturbations whose work constitutes a substantial fraction of the moon's orbital energy. Together, our results indicate that moons likely do not survive during a planet's high-eccentricity migration phase in a three-body configuration.
item.dc:creator: Ritvik Sai Narayan, Joseph R. Livesey, Juliette Becker

item.title: What Shapes the Ultraviolet Spectra of Type Ia Supernovae?
item.description: arXiv:2610.27807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) observations of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) exhibit significant diversity, but their physical origin remains poorly understood. We investigate UV spectra of SNe Ia observed with the Swift UltraViolet and Optical Telescope. Our expanded pre-maximum sample probes dependencies on decline rate, ejecta properties, and host environment. We recover the correlation between UV flux and decline rate near maximum in the near-UV (NUV), and find correlations at pre-maximum phases in both the NUV and mid-UV (MUV). This trend is strongly wavelength dependent, with slow decliners showing higher NUV but lower MUV flux than fast decliners. Synthetic TARDIS spectra varying the 56Ni abundance show that enhanced 56Ni suppresses the MUV while increasing the NUV, broadly reproducing the trend. We find no significant correlation between UV flux and ejecta velocity, while Si II 6355 pEW shows trends similar to those with decline rate. We also find no significant correlations with host-galaxy properties, although host environment may contribute to the remaining UV diversity among SNe with similar decline rates. Early-excess SNe show enhanced flux mainly in the NUV rather than a broad UV excess, suggesting that strong circumstellar interaction is not necessarily required to explain the observed excess emission. Peculiar subclasses show distinct UV properties, with brighter and hotter subclasses showing higher UV flux, although the current sample is small and does not cover all SN Ia subtypes. Our results suggest that the UV diversity of SNe Ia is shaped by multiple mechanisms that contribute differently across the UV wavelength range.
item.dc:creator: Snehasish Bhattacharjee, Yen-Chen Pan, Anirban Dutta, Shubham Gupta, Chia-Yu Cheng, Charles D. Kilpatrick, Matthew R. Siebert

item.title: The environments of type Ibn supernovae: evidence for a strong Wolf-Rayet star component
item.description: arXiv:2610.27931v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Characterisation of progenitor stars of supernovae (SNe) poses several challenges. Direct observations of progenitors are based on serendipitious archival observations and are only possible for nearby events. Indirect methods include inferring nickel mass from the light curves or oxygen masses from the SN's nebular phase, both of which are tools to constrain the progenitor's initial mass. Alternatively, environments of SNe have been used as a proxy for the progenitor's age and metallicity. The progenitor channel of type Ibn SNe is a hotly debated topic. The mass-loss and the formation of He-rich circumstellar medium requires strong envelope stripping of the progenitor star. For core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe), this requires strong stellar wind mass losses, i.e. a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star, or binary interaction with a companion star. Here, we analyse a sample of host galaxies of type Ibn SNe that have been observed with MUSE. We use H$\alpha$ emission to infer the transient's association to star formation and derive the local metallicity with commonly used strong line diagnostic. We find that the sample of SNe are highly associated with star formation in the host galaxy, typically situated within one of the brightest HII regions in the host galaxy. The NCR distribution of H$\alpha$ pixels in SN Ibn environments strongly resembles that of WR stars, and shows a stronger preference to SF compared to other core-collapse SN types. Metallicity measurements show typically sub-solar metallicity in the SN environments.
item.dc:creator: Timo Kravtsov, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Joseph P. Anderson

item.title: Constraining Solid HNCO and Its Environment in Open JWST Data with Laboratory Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2610.27949v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The presence of HNCO in the gaseous phase is well known for the interstellar medium, but the molecule is not detected yet in the solid phase. We report the first laboratory-confirmed identification of solid HNCO at 2260 cm$^{-1}$ in open JWST data using laboratory infrared spectra. For that, we grew binary mixtures of HNCO with main constituents of interstellar ice using ISEAge setup at 10 K: HNCO:H$_2$O = 1:10, HNCO:CO = 1:10, HNCO:CO$_2$ = 1:10, HNCO:CH$_3$OH~=~1:10. We present transmission infrared spectra of pure HNCO and HNCO-bearing ices along with the corresponding band strengths at 10 K. The fitting of open JWST observational data with the laboratory reference spectra in a 10--23 K temperature range show that solid HNCO is predominantly located in the apolar layer rich in CO. The abundance of solid HNCO is approximately estimated as 0.04--0.15\% relative to solid H$_2$O. The positive correlation between HNCO and N$_2$O suggests their co-formation via the chemical route that includes solid N$_2$. The results are also supported by the numerical modeling of HNCO formation in protostellar objects with predicted abundance of 0.06--0.11\%. We calculated the upper limits for CH$_3$CN toward two protostars and evaluated its abundance to solid water using the spectroscopic fitting and modeling.
item.dc:creator: Ruslan Nakibov (Research Laboratory for Astrochemistry, Ural Federal University, Yekaterinburg, Russia), Varvara Karteyeva (Research Laboratory for Astrochemistry, Ural Federal University, Yekaterinburg, Russia), Katerina Borshcheva (Research Laboratory for Astrochemistry, Ural Federal University, Yekaterinburg, Russia, Institute of Astronomy of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia), Igor Petrashkevich (Research Laboratory for Astrochemistry, Ural Federal University, Yekaterinburg, Russia), Mikhail Medvedev (Research Laboratory for Astrochemistry, Ural Federal University, Yekaterinburg, Russia), Anton Vasyunin (Research Laboratory for Astrochemistry, Ural Federal University, Yekaterinburg, Russia)

item.title: On the superbursts as photodisintegrators of ashes from the rp-process -- Numerical simulations of superbursts with MESA II
item.description: arXiv:2610.28049v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Context: Superbursts are energetic explosions in the crusts of neutron stars in Low-Mass X-ray Binaries (LMXBs). At temperatures above 4 GK, photodisintegration of heavy rp-process ashes may play a major role alongside $^{12}$C fusion. Aims: We investigate how photodisintegration of rp-process ashes affects superburst properties and the initial $^{12}$C abundance required for ignition. Methods: We simulate superbursts with MESA v.24.08.1. Besides the canonical fuel of $20\%$ $^{12}$C and $80\%$ $^{56}$Fe, we test different $^{12}$C abundances mixed with scaled rp-process ashes. Results: Superbursts can ignite with only $10\%$ $^{12}$C when the remaining $90\%$ consists of rp-process ashes. Their luminosity is comparable to that of the canonical fuel, whereas $10\%$ $^{12}$C mixed with $90\%$ $^{56}$Fe yields lower luminosity. $^{56}$Fe remains the most abundant ash nuclide. Although photodisintegration drives nucleosynthesis, neutron, proton and alpha captures release energy at late times. We also find that $A=64$ nuclides or $^{20}$Ne help reduce the $^{12}$C abundance needed for ignition. Conclusions: The composition of accreted material - not just its $^{12}$C content - substantially affects superburst ignition, luminosity and nucleosynthesis.
item.dc:creator: M. Nava-Callejas, S. Goriely, N. Chamel

item.title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.28424v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.
item.dc:creator: B. Tripathi, A. E. Fraser, P. W. Terry, E. G. Zweibel, M. J. Pueschel, A. M. Beloborodov

item.title: A Solar Optical Clock
item.description: arXiv:2610.28485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Connor Fredrick, Ryan K. Cole, Ryan Terrien, Suvrath Mahadevan, Scott A. Diddams

item.title: A sub-Earth-sized TESS planet candidate in the nearby M-dwarf binary GJ 774, most likely orbiting GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274)
item.description: arXiv:2610.28575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small planets transiting the nearest M dwarfs are the terrestrial planets most accessible to detailed characterisation. We report a sub-Earth-sized transiting planet candidate in the wide (17.6") M-dwarf binary GJ 774 at 12.86 pc, most likely orbiting the M2.5 primary GJ 774 A (TIC 351339274). The signal was a SPOC multi-sector threshold-crossing event (MES = 7.95) and is not a TESS Object of Interest. In eight TESS sectors (2019-2026) a 1.28-h transit recurs every 4.225138 +/- 0.000010 d with a box-mean depth of 365 +/- 32 ppm in A's light. The 2026 data, which entered neither the SPOC search nor our selection, show it at the ephemeris predicted from 2019-2023 data (304 +/- 43 ppm; none of 10^5 phase-scrambled versions of the 2026 data is as deep). The per-target false-alarm probability is < 0.03 at 95%. Odd/even, secondary-eclipse, archival-plate and Gaia radial-velocity tests exclude unrelated blended eclipsing binaries and eclipsing companions on 4.2-d orbits, and hierarchical eclipsing binaries are improbable. The stars are 0.85 TESS pixel apart, so the TRICERATOPS false-positive probability (0.26) is set by a planet on GJ 774 B. B is disfavoured because its own light does not dim enough: PRF-deblended photometry gives 109 +/- 115 ppm in B's light, against 1089 ppm required if B were the host. Conditional on a point source at A or at B, the joint host model gives P(A)=0.59-0.97 (0.97 for the native target-pixel baseline). Over all sectors the PRF photometry is consistent with A, but in the out-of-sample 2026 data 40% of the deficit appears at B's position, an unexplained 2-3 sigma (PSF-model and depth dependent) tension with host A. On A the planet has R_p=0.70 +/- 0.06 R_Earth, S=15.0 +/- 1.8 S_Earth and T_eq=548 +/- 16 K. It is not validated; resolved ground-based photometry of the pair would test host B directly.
item.dc:creator: Jaden Tripp

item.title: Formation and Evolution of [Wolf-Rayet] Planetary Nebulae through a Late Thermal Pulse
item.description: arXiv:2603.26536v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present the first radiation-hydrodynamical simulations of the formation of a born-again planetary nebula (PN) triggered by a late thermal pulse (LTP). The 2D radiation-hydrodynamic simulations, performed with the {\sc pluto} code, have been consistently coupled to stellar evolution calculations using the Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics ({\sc mesa}) code. Very particularly the stellar evolution model uses (i) updated opacity tables for H-deficient, C-rich mixtures during the LTP, and (ii) a mass-loss prescription tailored for H-deficient [Wolf-Rayet]([WR])-type winds during the post-LTP phase. Our stellar model reproduces the nearly complete depletion of H expected after an LTP event, while matching the observed abundances and spectral types of iconic [WR]-type central stars of PNe. The simulations show for the first time that the H-deficient LTP ejecta forms a transient double-shell structure which, after $\sim$1000 yr, becomes fully mixed with the H-rich PN. The ejecta mass ($\sim3.4\times10^{-4}$~M$_\odot$) is too small to leave a lasting imprint on the nebular abundances, predicting H-rich PNe around [WR] central stars. The injection of LTP material into the hot bubble drives turbulence, clump formation, and enhanced mixing, providing an explanation to the larger expansion velocities and larger turbulent nebular structures of PNe with [WR] central stars compared to those with H-rich central stars. These results provide robust support for the born-again scenario as the origin of H-deficient [WR] central stars within H-rich PNe.
item.dc:creator: J. B. Rodr\'iguez-Gonz\'alez, R. Orozco-Duarte, J. A. Toal\'a, M. M. Miller Bertolami, H. Todt, M. A. Guerrero, L. Conmy, R. Kuiper

item.title: Periodic activity on the (sub)mm surface of the AGB star Mira A
item.description: arXiv:2608.23724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evolved stars on the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) lose mass through stellar winds launched from their dynamic extended atmospheres. Recent high-angular-resolution observations of the archetypal AGB star Mira A (o Ceti) have revealed compact hotspots on its (sub)millimetre surface, whose origin remains unclear. We aim to characterise the (sub)millimetre photosphere of Mira A and investigate the properties and temporal behaviour of the compact hotspots detected on its surface. We analysed 19 epochs of high-angular-resolution observations obtained with ALMA in Bands 4, 6, 7, and 9. The complex visibilities were fitted with parametric models to derive the flux density, size, morphology, and brightness temperature of the stellar disc and an additional, more compact component across multiple pulsation phases and observing frequencies. Our results show that, near maximum light, the flux density of the stellar disc increases with frequency while its apparent size decreases, in agreement with the expected stratified radio photosphere. In Band 6, both the flux density and the size of the stellar disc appear to vary with pulsation phase, with the largest measured values occurring close to optical maximum light and the lowest observed around minimum light. Compact hotspots are detected in Bands 6 and 7 near maximum light, with their brightness temperatures exceeding those of the stellar disc by several thousand kelvin and reaching a temperature excess of ~8200 K in Band 6. They are highly energetic and are detected over timescales of weeks, while the available observations also suggest potential longer-term changes in both their position and intensity. Hotspot activity appears to occur repeatedly across multiple pulsation cycles and may be linked to strong shocks, magnetic activity, and/or episodic mass ejections, and could therefore play an important role in the mass-loss process in AGB stars.
item.dc:creator: M. Andriantsaralaza, B. Bojnordi Arbab, W. Vlemmings, T. Khouri, L. Planquart, K. T. Wong, J. Alcolea, E. Humphreys, S. del Palacio, M. Wittkowski

item.title: Solar spicule population properties inferred from IRIS Mg II k off-limb spectra using likelihood-free Bayesian inference
item.description: arXiv:2609.37811v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Solar spicules are ubiquitous and strongly overlap in off-limb observations, which complicates the interpretation of individual events. We aim to infer population-level properties of spicules from IRIS Mg II k off-limb spectra using a forward model that explicitly accounts for line-of-sight superposition and instrumental effects. We constructed a stochastic 3D spicule-population model and synthesized Mg II k spectra with radiative transfer, including instrumental degradation and photon noise. We then constrained the hyperparameters that describe the underlying spicule population with likelihood-free Bayesian inference. This approach combines approximate Bayesian computation and an adaptive population Monte Carlo sampler, comparing observed and simulated datasets through principal-component summary statistics at five heights above the limb. The inferred posterior constrains effective population-level properties of the spicules that dominate the observed Mg II k variability and height dependence. These constraints provide a route to connect off-limb spectroscopy with forthcoming spectropolarimetric diagnostics of the chromosphere--corona interface.
item.dc:creator: Jiri Stepan, Stanislav Gunar, Akiko Tei, Petr Heinzel

item.title: Kratos-polrad: Novel GPU system for Monte-Carlo simulations with consistent polarization calculations
item.description: arXiv:2512.01283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Polarized radiation serves as a vital diagnostic tool in astrophysics, providing unique insights into magnetic field geometries, scattering processes, and three-dimensional structures in diverse astrophysical scenarios. To address these applications, we present Kratos_polrad, a novel GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo Radiative Transfer code built upon the heterogeneous computing framework of Kratos, designed for self-consistent and efficient polarization calculations. It utilizes a comprehensive treatment of the Stokes parameters throughout photon propagation, featuring grain-lab frame transformations using quaternion algebra and a consistent analytical integration of polarized extinction and emission within each cell, which are useful in modeling radiative transfer processes with scatterings by aligned dust grains. The code implements two-step polarimetry imaging that decouples Monte Carlo sampling of scattering physics from imaging geometry, enabling efficient synthesis maximizing the utilization of photon packets. Extensive validation against analytical solutions and established codes demonstrates accurate treatment of diverse polarization phenomena, including self-scattering polarization, dichroic extinction in aligned dust grains, and complex polarization patterns in twisted magnetic field configurations. By leveraging massive GPU parallelism, optimized memory access patterns, and analytical approaches for optically thick cells, Kratos_polrad achieves performance improvements of ~10^2 times compared to CPU-based methods, enabling previously prohibitive studies in polarimetric astrophysics.
item.dc:creator: Haifeng Yang, Lile Wang

item.title: The Life and Death of Stars That Capture Primordial Black Holes
item.description: arXiv:2606.02700v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window ($10^{17}-10^{23}\,{\rm g}$) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars. We develop the first global framework for the evolution of stars that capture PBHs, combining analytic calculations, stellar evolution models, 3D general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, and Monte Carlo population synthesis. We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly. Capture is dominated by three-body interactions with planetary or stellar companions. For a solar-type host with a Jupiter analog, inspiral within a main-sequence lifetime requires $M_{\rm BH}^{\rm crit}\gtrsim 10^{22}\,{\rm g}$, while lighter PBHs generally require tighter companions. Once deposited at the center, the PBH grows through inefficient quasi-spherical Bondi accretion; if it reaches the angular-momentum threshold before consuming the host, the inflow circularizes into a disk. Our Monte Carlo calculations yield sizable quiet-consumption and explosive-disruption populations, with final PBH masses $M_{\rm BH}\sim0.01-1\,M_\odot$ and disk-forming PBH spins $a_\ast\approx0.8$. Disk formation is the point of no return: disk winds and relativistic jets of $\sim10^{45}-10^{50}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ disrupt the star within minutes. The resulting transients may include a $\sim$day-long UV/blue signal, radio afterglow, and, if the jet escapes, an X-ray-flash/low-luminosity gamma-ray-burst (XRF/llGRB) signal. For an $O(1)$ PBH dark matter fraction and optimistic capture assumptions, the event rate can reach that of llGRBs. The low-mass, high-spin remnants offer a complementary PBH probe and possible source for subsolar BH mergers.
item.dc:creator: Ore Gottlieb, Matteo Cantiello, Cameron Norton, Ken Van Tilburg, Matthew Kleban

item.title: Exact 1D Nonlinear Solutions for Proton-Driven Plasma Wakefields
item.description: arXiv:2607.06458v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We extend the classical 1D nonlinear relativistic plasma wakefield paradigm to evaluate the pristine fluid profiles driven by intense relativistic proton trains under the comoving coordinate approximation. Using an intense two-bunch scheme, our adaptive integration model is validated down to machine precision against exact closed-form cold-fluid invariants, confirming that interface boundary corners represent physical step discontinuities in the second potential derivative. Scaling to an $N=100$ micro-bunch train, we resolve macroscopic phase-accumulation and subsequent nonlinear detuning by deriving a closed-form, parameter-free piecewise analytical envelope expression. This solution successfully maps the initial unattenuated quadratic coherent growth alongside the flat asymptotic horizontal saturation horizon governed by nonlinear energy conservation. Furthermore, the framework analytically evaluates the transient envelope overshoot, tracking its decay onto the saturation boundary via an exact phase-slip integration length scale. Providing immediate, ready macro-envelope bounds, this computationally inexpensive tool eliminates empirical adjustments and yields a robust mathematical baseline designed to guide and accelerate complex, multi-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations through rapid parameter space exploration before deploying heavy computational assets. It establishes an efficient foundation to optimize asymmetric, custom-shaped driver profiles required to break the fundamental symmetric transformer ratio limit of 2 to make current particle accelerators more efficient.
item.dc:creator: D. Tsiklauri

item.title: Unveiling the Milky Way with a Gaia DR3 census of OB-type stars within 2 kpc. I. Tracing local Galactic structure, massive star-forming regions and core-collapse supernova progenitors
item.description: arXiv:2607.07068v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: O- and B-type stars are young and hot, thereby serving as vital tracers of the star formation and spiral arm structure of the Milky Way. At the dusk of the \textit{Gaia} DR3 era, a high-confidence and accurate catalogue appears timely. We have characterized 105,971 OB-type stars (T$_{\rm eff} >$ 10,000 K) within 2 kpc from the Sun, using an astro-photometric Bayesian inference tool. Our map unveils a complex view of the young stellar populations across the thin disk, with prominent large-scale features such as the Cepheus Spur, the Giant Oval Cavity, and a segment the Sagittarius-Carina arm all visible. Their inhomogeneous spatial distribution implies that massive star formation has taken place clustered across a few highly concentrated regions. We find a correlation between the overdensities of OB-type stars and young open clusters, and attribute departure from it to extinction effects. We identify 4200 stars as model-dependent core-collapse supernova (ccSN) or direct-collapse black hole (BH) progenitor candidates, including 6 ccSN progenitor candidates within 125 pc -- the maximum radius within which a ccSN explosion could be harmful to Earth's biosphere -- but our analysis suggests none of them exploding within the next 5 Myrs. Finally, we anticipate more evolved OB-type stars to collapse to form BHs within the next 1 Myr than ccSN progenitors will explode, despite the former's much scarcer number. A possible interpretation is a recent star formation burst in the local Milky Way, consistent with overdensities of ccSN progenitor candidates in Cyg OB2 and the Sagittarius-Carina arm.
item.dc:creator: Alexis L. Quintana, Kiril Maltsev, Eloisa Poggio, Emily L. Hunt, Nicholas J. Wright, Sara R. Berlanas, Laia Casamiquela, Abel de Burgos, Hanna Parul, Misha Haywood, Paola Di Matteo, Chervin Laporte, Juan Mart\'inez Garc\'ia
